key_claims: The CIA's plan to capture Bin Ladin with Afghan tribal fighters was judged too risky in spring 1998 and not recommended for approval.
Clinton signed successive authorizations for offensive CIA operations against Bin Ladin after the East Africa bombings.
CIA Afghan proxies reported about half a dozen aborted opportunities to attack Bin Ladin's convoy before 9/11.
The Taliban regime was not inclined to cooperate on Bin Ladin, and the US had no officers in Afghanistan, which limited rendition.
The Bush administration's 2001 policy review shifted emphasis from the Northern Alliance toward anti-Taliban Pashtuns.
Tenet's position deferred reconnaissance Predator flights in spring 2001 pending the armed version.
The CIA read Clinton's authorities as requiring capture of Bin Ladin, while NSC staff believed the intent was to kill him.
No CIA official complained to the White House that the authorities were unclear or restrictive.
The CIA relied on Afghan tribal fighters and Massoud's Northern Alliance as proxies with limited confidence in their paramilitary skills.
Tenet estimated the CIA's odds of success in Afghanistan before 9/11 at 10 to 20 percent.
The Bush administration's 2001 policy review shifted emphasis toward anti-Taliban Pashtuns, with a plan finalized only around Sept 4-10, 2001.
The armed Predator was rushed in 2001 but was not ready by 9/11, with unresolved command and control issues.
